newsitem.title: ISRAEL: British teens recovering from Israeli Arab attack.
newsitem.headline: British teens recovering from Israeli Arab attack.

text.p: Just hours after stepping off a plane from London, 16-year-old Graham Kogan was running down a Jaffa street chased by an Israeli Arab man brandishing a Samurai sword.
"I thought he was going to cut me to death. I thought I was going to die," Kogan said on Wednesday.
The youngster was among a group of 40 British Jewish teens who arrived in Israel on Tuesday for a four-week "Israel Experience" tour sponsored by the quasi-governmental Jewish Agency.
They got a lesson in the turmoil of the Middle East at the start of what the Jewish Agency billed as an educational tour.

An Israeli Arab who police said was bent on avenging the pasting in the West Bank town of Hebron of a poster depicting the prophet Mohammad as a pig, rammed his car into the group, slightly injuring eight people.
He then ran down the street towards sidewalk cafes, stabbing a woman and a youth. Their wounds were not life-threatening.
"I can imagine from the trauma and the tragedy, they will get a lot of strong feelings about Israel," said Shlomo Gravitz of the Jewish Agency.
Danny Consul, an off-duty border policeman who detained the assailant, said the Israeli Arab suddenly got out of the car "holding a sword in one hand and a commando knife in the other".
The assailant "swiped at several people and even hit a few," Consul said. "I pointed a gun at him and said 'Stop! Police! Get on the floor'."
Kogan said he had no intention of cutting short his visit.
"I still want to carry on," he said.
The 15- to 17-year-olds, one in a cast and on crutches and others with elasticated bandages around their legs, spent Wednesday recuperating in a Tel Aviv youth hostel.
"The police investigation of the suspect...reveals that the background of the deed was national and religious," police spokeswoman Linda Menuhin said.
"The man said he was affected by the poster against Mohammad and he wanted to protect Islam by his deeds," she said.

An Israeli woman supporter of the outlawed anti-Arab Kach movement has admitted putting the crudely drawn pig placards on some 20 Hebron storefronts three weeks ago. She has been charged with racial incitement and membership in a terrorist group.
Tel Aviv district police commander Shlomo Aharonishki said the attacker came from the Galilee town of Nazareth.
"He is not cooperating with us at present," Aharonishki said. "The only thing he says is that he doesn't know what happened and can't remember what happened."
A man identified by Israel's army radio as the attacker's brother denied media reports he was a Moslem extremist.

"This is something that's really shocked us and the background to it is not nationalist. This is simply a man who has a few problems at home with the family and I think that's what led him to do this," he told the radio.
